title: Street-Level Inclusion
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Drawing on Michael Lipsky's 'street-level bureaucracy' theory -- that frontline workers like teachers are de facto policymakers because their daily interpretive choices determine what a policy actually becomes in practice -- this essay examines the UK's newest instruction to teachers, 'teach more inclusively,' and argues its vagueness is a genuine problem, not merely an implementation detail. Evans identifies that education policy has historically asked teachers two distinct things (become a generally better teacher; become a better teacher of a specific subject), and argues the inclusion agenda introduces a third, subtly different framing that foregrounds pupil diversity itself as the starting point, which forces genuine trade-offs in limited department-meeting time between discussing subject-specific pedagogy and discussing pupil needs profiles -- trade-offs he stresses are empirical questions currently being settled by ideology rather than evidence. The piece's most substantive content comes from a researchED session by Becky Allen (inspired by Craig Barton's podcast) arguing that how much a specific pedagogical choice matters varies enormously by both subject content (a pizza-slice fraction analogy helps at primary level but limits later manipulation of fractions) and by learner (well-prepared students can 'repair' poor teaching, while disadvantaged learners are more sensitive to instructional choices) -- implying the most genuinely inclusive policy response might be identifying precisely where teaching choices matter most, rather than issuing a blanket instruction to reconsider all pedagogy through a diversity lens. Evans closes by predicting that subject-specific pedagogy will not be the actual focus of the coming inclusion policy push, and that -- per Lipsky's framework -- it will ultimately be individual teachers' street-level interpretive choices, not the policy's stated intent, that determine what 'more inclusive teaching' comes to mean in practice.
points: Lipsky's 'street-level bureaucracy' framework reframes teachers as de facto policymakers whose daily interpretive choices, not a policy's stated intent, determine what any instruction to 'teach differently' actually becomes in practice -- meaning the coming inclusion agenda's real content will be decided by individual teachers, not policymakers.

The essay identifies a genuine, previously-unnamed category shift: education policy has historically asked teachers to become generally better, or better within a specific subject, but 'teach more inclusively' introduces a third framing that starts from pupil diversity itself, forcing real trade-offs in limited department time between subject-pedagogy discussion and pupil-needs-profile discussion.

Becky Allen's pizza-slice fractions example demonstrates that pedagogical choices matter differently depending on downstream use: a concrete analogy that successfully teaches primary-level unit-fraction understanding actively limits a student's later ability to manipulate fractions algebraically in secondary school.

The claim that disadvantaged learners may be more sensitive to specific instructional choices while well-prepared students can 'repair' poor teaching reframes inclusion itself as potentially requiring identification of where teaching choices matter most, rather than a uniform mandate to reconsider all pedagogy through a diversity lens.
quotes: In Michael Lipsky's classic book, Street-Level Bureaucracy, he argues that those on the frontline of public services -- teachers, social workers, nurses -- are de facto policymakers, such is their power to control what is enacted every day when policy meets reality.

Too often, practitioners will adopt the visible features of the change intended without internalising the underlying methodology or rationale. This impression of fidelity satisfies policy makers but fails to lead to higher quality because a vital ingredient is missing: an improvement in expert decision making.
These are empirical questions. Unfortunately, policy is driven by ideology, not evidence.

Becky provided the example of the teaching of fractions in primary schools where the concrete analogy given is often the slices of a pizza. This approach helps pupils understand a unit can be divided into parts, but is limiting when the pupil is asked to manipulate fractions in secondary school.

Pupils with good prior knowledge may be able to 'repair' poor teaching, whereas disadvantaged learners may be highly sensitive to instructional choices. If true, the most inclusive thing we could do may be to work out when teaching matters most and work towards aligning teaching practices in these specific respects.
What Lipsky teaches us is that it is the street-level bureaucrats who will decide what happens next.
